prize_parts.citation: For the invention and realisation of the optical lattice clock, based on magic-wavelength trapping of many atoms, and its development to the 10^-18 level of fractional uncertainty

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged from round 1: B001 alone, credited to Katori and Ye. After reading all eight round-1 statements, the case looks stronger to me than before, because the objections raised against it are the same in every file and none of them is a scientific doubt about the result. The magic-wavelength lattice is a distinct idea: it cancels the light shift of the clock transition while trapping many atoms, which removes Doppler and recoil shifts and lets one interrogate thousands of atoms at once. Katori proposed and first realised it, and Ye's group showed how far systematic control and coherence can be pushed, to about 10^-18, with many-body effects in the clock becoming something one has to understand. Independent laboratories reproduce this and compare clocks across sites, and the consequences can be checked by nature: gravitational redshift over millimetres to centimetres, bounds on varying constants and on ultralight dark-matter couplings. As a theorist who works next to experimentalists, I value that the result was understood detail by detail, and I think this is the maturity criterion that matters. I do not make timing depend on the redefinition of the SI second, which is a metrological decision that follows the physics. On the question of a second part, I do not see an alternative that is ready, and I prefer a clean one-part prize to a two-part prize that is only a compromise.
statement.case_against: The strongest objection remains that the lattice clock may be read as a refinement of the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 prize for control of single quantum systems and ion clocks. I think the answer is in the wording of the citation, which must name the many-atom magic-wavelength scheme and not optical clocks or precision in general. Second, a two-name credit leaves out the Paris, NIST/Boulder, PTB and other groups that made decisive contributions to specific milestones, and none of us has checked the priority record for the first strontium lattice clock against the 10^-18 result. Third, the 10^-18 figure can be called a record in systematic control, and the weight of the case therefore rests on the scheme and on the physics it has opened, not on the number itself. I cannot fully rule these out from my own expertise, which is in superconducting circuits and not in metrology.

responses.point: Olsson asks whether the 10^-18 headline is a discovery about nature or a record in systematic control, and suggests the case depends on whether the magic-wavelength proposal and the first lattice clock are the invention, rather than the later accuracy record.
responses.response: I think your test is the right one and it favours B001. The invention is the magic-wavelength lattice, and I would put it first in the citation. But I would not separate it from Ye's work: at 10^-18 the clock became a different instrument, one where collisional and many-body shifts, blackbody radiation and coherence had to be understood quantitatively before one could trust gravitational redshift over a millimetre. That is physics about how interacting atoms in a lattice behave and not only engineering. So I keep the citation wording as invention plus development, with the lattice scheme as the grammatical subject. I do not agree that this is closer to a record than to a discovery, but I accept that the phrase about 10^-18 should be secondary to the scheme.

responses.point: Danielsson, as Secretary, wants external expert reports on the priority record, and asks that the citation stress the lattice concept and its consequences, since other groups (SYRTE, NIST, PTB) were decisive for specific milestones.
responses.response: I agree that an external expert check on priority is a sensible step before the vote, since I have also not verified it and my own field is far from clocks. I would not make the vote wait for it, because every one of us names the same pair and nobody has produced a competing priority claim that would change the names. If a report did show that a third person has a claim to the invention of the magic-wavelength scheme, I would reconsider the third name, since the cap allows one more. Until then, I would rather treat the other clock groups as essential contributors to a mature field than as co-discoverers, which is the usual treatment of reproduction and refinement. This is also why I do not favour a citation that mentions precision alone, as you say.

responses.point: Kroll ranks B001 first and raises whether a two-part prize adding B042 or B003 would improve the configuration or only dilute it, given the three-person limit, and notes that my WACQT role overlaps with his own at Chalmers.
responses.response: On a second part, I think it would dilute it. B042 has five credited names and, as Lindroth and I both said, any three cut a founder, so it fails the exact-credit test that B001 passes easily. For B003, I confirm my disclosure and keep my recusal: I will not argue for or against it. I also take your point that our WACQT link is only relevant to the circuit candidates, and I have taken B003 out of my alternatives, so my preferences cannot be read as lobbying for my own field. My view is that the committee should treat B001 on its own merits and leave other candidates for later years.

responses.point: Lindroth notes that seven of eight members rank B001 and that credit is wider than two names, but she regards the objections as real qualifications and not disqualifying, and she discloses a field-level connection to B001 and B042 through atomic theory.
responses.response: I agree with your reading, and I appreciate that you disclosed the field-level link, since you are the member best placed to judge whether the atomic-physics community would see Katori and Ye as the decisive pair. I would ask you, as the AMO expert, to say directly whether you consider the lattice clock to be distinct in principle from the 2012 prize for ion-trap control. My reading is that the Haroche-Wineland work was about controlling and measuring individual quantum systems, while the lattice clock is about using a large ensemble in a way that reaches a statistical advantage and a new systematic regime, so the physical idea differs. If you disagree, that is the point on which my support for a one-part B001 would be most worth testing.

responses.point: Mehlig moved from B006 to B001 and keeps B006 and B004 as alternatives, and he recalls the 2D melting history from memory without having verified priority or the role of first-order melting.
responses.response: I appreciate the candour about your own first choice. I still defer on B006 and cannot judge the hexatic evidence, but your own caveat about system-dependent and first-order melting is, in my view, the reason it should stay an alternative for now. I note that I have left B004 and B010 out of my own alternatives, because the topological-insulator credit is split among Kane, Mele, Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang, Molenkamp, Hasan and Xue, which the three-name cap cannot represent, as you and Eriksson both say. That is the same exact-credit problem I find in B042, and it separates those candidates from B001.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts the magic-wavelength lattice clock as a distinct discovery from the 2005 and 2012 prizes, which turns on the wording of the citation.

Priority of the magic-wavelength proposal and the first strontium lattice clock against the contributions of other groups, which nobody on the committee has independently verified and which an external reviewer could settle.
Whether a third name would be warranted if an external report found a decisive contribution to the invention of the scheme.
Whether the pending redefinition of the SI second will change how the committee weighs the practical benefit, though I treat it as not decisive for the scientific case.
How soon a circuit QED prize could be considered after the 2025 prize, on which I am recused and cannot advise.
statement.conflict_note: I maintain my round-1 disclosure: I work in superconducting circuits and waveguide QED, direct the Wallenberg Centre for Quantum Technology, and have Chalmers colleagues and WACQT guest researchers in the field, so I am recused from deliberating on B003 and I have removed it from my alternatives. I also note that Stefan Kroll and Eva Olsson share an institutional link to my own, which is not relevant for B001, B042 or B017. I have no specific connection to Katori, Ye or the credited names of B042 and B017.
